title: Heat-triggered phospholipid flipping stabilizes plasma membrane fluidity.
journal: Nature 655(8124):1060-, 1 July 2026 (PMID 42386963; PMC13391374; Europe PMC isOpenAccess = Y, hasSuppl = Y; licence CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)
data_url: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC13391374/supplementaryFiles (9 files, 23,531,314 bytes uncompressed; the two 'Source Data' workbooks are 41586_2026_10726_MOESM8_ESM.xlsx and MOESM9_ESM.xlsx)

verified.what_i_actually_checked: I downloaded and opened every spreadsheet this paper has. (1) Europe PMC search on the DOI returned 1 hit, PMID 42386963 / PMC13391374, hasSuppl = 'Y'. (2) I pulled the full text XML (262,013 bytes) and parsed it: 9 supplementary-material elements, 56 section titles, a Data availability section and a Code availability section. (3) Direct download from PubMed Central was blocked by a proof-of-work cookie challenge ('Preparing to download ...', HTTP 403/404 with HTML), so I used the Europe PMC supplementary-files endpoint, which returned a 23,531,314-byte archive of all 9 files. (4) I opened all six .xlsx files by parsing the spreadsheet XML directly. Verified counts: Supplementary Table 1 (primers) 91 rows; Supplementary Table 2 (heat treatment conditions) 23 rows; Supplementary Table 3 (rice varieties used for expression) 36 variety rows across 7 haplotype groups; Supplementary Table 4 (orthologue sequence identity) 62 rows for OsALA5 and 58 for OsALIS2; Source Data Figs 1-5 = 5 sheets, 542 spreadsheet rows, 5,270 numeric cells; Source Data Extended Data Figs 1-10 = 10 sheets, 610 spreadsheet rows, 7,212 numeric cells. Total 12,482 numeric cells across roughly 35 separate figure panels. (5) NCBI elink from PubMed 42386963 to GEO DataSets, SRA, BioProject, BioSample, Nucleotide and Protein returned an empty linkset for all six. (6) Zenodo application programming interface search on the DOI returned 0 records; a search for 'OsALA5' returned 0 records. (7) I confirmed a data-quality defect by eye in Supplementary Table 3: the rice variety IRIS_313-9924 is listed twice, once as haplotype 3 with expression 8.14 plus or minus 0.08 and once as haplotype 6 with expression 5.70 plus or minus 0.08.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The biology and the experimental design. OsALA5 is a rice lipid pump (a P4-ATPase, an enzyme that uses ATP to move phospholipids from one face of a membrane to the other); with its partner protein OsALIS2 it moves saturated phosphatidylcholine to the inner face of the cell's outer membrane within minutes of heat exposure, which keeps the membrane from becoming too fluid. The haplotype survey of 2,236 Asian cultivated rice varieties was done against the third-party RiceVarMap v2.0 database, not re-verified by me; that database's own contents were not downloaded. Field-trial descriptions ('multi-year, multi-location') come from the text; the deposited source data contain only chamber and greenhouse panels plus two paddy-field panels. The MutMap gene-mapping whole-genome resequencing (about 25-fold depth) has no accession number anywhere in the article and did not appear in any NCBI link, so those reads are effectively not available.

a1_downloadable.note: PASSES. All 9 supplementary files download without login from the Europe PMC supplementary-files endpoint (23,531,314 bytes total; largest single file 17.36 MB, a PDF of uncropped gels). Note for the pipeline: PubMed Central's own /bin/ links now sit behind a proof-of-work browser challenge and return HTML, so Europe PMC is the working route.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAILS, and this is the killer. The two Source Data workbooks are not datasets; they are the numbers behind each figure panel, stacked vertically with a caption row, a units row and then one row per genotype with replicate values spread sideways across columns (for example 'ED Fig. 2f | Plant height (cm) | Control ... Heat ...' then 'Kas | 111 | 117 | 116 | ...'). There is no column that any model could predict. To get a label you would have to decide which of roughly 35 incommensurable readouts counts as the outcome, unpivot each panel by hand, and invent a row key. The thing being predicted would have to be built from scratch.

a3_inputs_present.note: FAILS too. There are no input features of any kind: no sequences, no SMILES chemical strings, no genotype matrix, no gene expression matrix. The only 'feature' available per row is a genotype nickname such as 'Kas', 'OsALA5-KO1' or 'CL' and a temperature. Supplementary Table 4 lists 62 OsALA5 orthologues by Phytozome gene identifier with a percent-identity number, but not their amino-acid sequences, so even a sequence model would need 62 lookups in an external database first.

a4_units_stated.note: PASSES, and this is the one genuinely good thing about these files. Every panel block carries its units in the caption cell: 'Survival rate (%)', 'ATPase activity (nM Pi/min/ug)', 'mol% cytoplasmic PC (18:0/18:0)', 'LysoPS content (x10-5 umol/mg protein)', 'Plant height (cm)', '1000-grain weight (g)'. The catch is that units live in merged header cells read by humans, not in a units column read by a program.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAILS badly. Verified by opening the files: 542 spreadsheet rows in Source Data Figs 1-5 plus 610 in Source Data Extended Data Figs 1-10, i.e. 1,152 rows total, and most of those are caption, header or blank spacer rows. The 12,482 numeric cells are split across about 35 unrelated assays with 2 to 40 replicates each; the largest single coherent block is one agronomy panel with about 30 plants per genotype. The checklist floor is roughly 1,500 labelled rows for regression or 400 for classification, for one task. No task here reaches 400.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: 0.024 GB (the six .xlsx files total 267,508 bytes; the whole supplementary bundle is 23.5 MB)
a6_fits_laptop.note: Trivially fits on any laptop. Irrelevant, because there is nothing to model.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Mostly consistent, with one defect I found by opening the file. The 7 haplotypes in Supplementary Table 3 match the 'seven OsALA5 haplotypes' in the Fig. 5b caption, and the treatment conditions in Supplementary Table 2 match the figure panels they point to. But Supplementary Table 3 lists the rice variety IRIS_313-9924 twice, under haplotype 3 and under haplotype 6, with different expression values, which cannot both be right. The paper's 2,236-variety haplotype survey could not be checked because those genotypes live in the third-party RiceVarMap v2.0 database.

a8_label_provenance.note: PASSES on provenance, which is the one Part A test this paper would survive cleanly. Every number traces to a direct physical measurement: plants scored alive or dead after a heat chamber run, fluorescence anisotropy of membrane dyes, inorganic phosphate release in an ATPase assay, mol% of named lipid species from liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, conductivity for ion leakage, grain weighed on a balance. Nothing is another model's output and nothing is computed from the features.

existing_models.name: Attribute-weighting plus Naive Bayes classifier for P-type ATPase substrate specificity (Niazi and co-workers, Physiology and Molecular Biology of Plants, 2016; doi 10.1007/s12298-016-0351-5). P-type ATPases are the pump family that OsALA5 belongs to; the model guesses what each pump transports from amino-acid composition alone.
existing_models.score_and_split: The abstract (retrieved from the Europe PMC application programming interface, not the full text) reports predicting the substrate specificity of two uncharacterised Arabidopsis pumps, UniProt accessions Q9LVV1 and O22180, with '100 % prediction confidence'. No held-out test set, no cross-validation scheme and no dataset size are stated in the abstract. A confidence figure is not an accuracy figure, so this is effectively an unevaluated model.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: The abstract says existing predictors need 'further investigation ... to improve the efficiency and performance', i.e. the authors themselves treat accurate substrate prediction for this family as open. I did not retrieve the discussion section.

existing_models.name: Deep-learning genomic prediction for rice traits (Marco Lozano and co-workers, Plant Methods, 2024; doi 10.1186/s13007-024-01250-y). Predicts crop traits from genome-wide genetic markers, comparing multilayer perceptron and convolutional neural networks against Bayesian linear models.
existing_models.score_and_split: Abstract retrieved from Europe PMC: combining structural variants with single-nucleotide markers improved prediction in 87% of cases, and deep-learning models beat Bayesian models in 75% of cases across four traits and two validation strategies. The abstract reports win rates, not absolute accuracies, and does not name the split sizes. I did not retrieve the full text.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: The abstract frames the open question as whether deep learning helps when training and target sets are not closely related, which is the generalisation-to-unrelated-varieties problem.

existing_models.name: Machine-learning classification of gel versus fluid lipid states in simulated bilayers (Walter and co-workers, Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics, 2020; arXiv 1907.05788). Closest existing model to the membrane-fluidity question this paper raises.
existing_models.score_and_split: Known to me only from a web search result listing (title, journal, arXiv identifier). It classifies individual lipid configurations from molecular dynamics simulations near the phase transition of a single lipid, dipalmitoyl-phosphatidylcholine. I did not retrieve the abstract or full text, so I report no score and no split.

c2_audit.note: This is a partial audit. I ran it only to see whether a worthwhile project existed near this paper before confirming the Part A failure. The picture is that substrate-specificity prediction for lipid pumps is genuinely under-modelled (an opening), but this paper supplies none of the data such a model would need.

backbone.name: ESM-2, a protein language model that turns an amino-acid sequence into a numeric vector, would be the right backbone for the only interesting task here (guess a lipid pump's cargo from its sequence). It cannot be used, because the paper deposits 62 gene identifiers and a percent-identity number, not 62 sequences, and supplies no cargo labels.
backbone.hardware: Not assessed. For reference, embedding a few hundred plant P4-ATPase sequences with the small 8-million-parameter ESM-2 checkpoint would take minutes on a laptop CPU, but the labels do not exist.
backbone.licence: The article is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives), which explicitly forbids sharing adapted material derived from the article. That is an awkward licence for a derived dataset even if one existed.

integration.partner_dataset: Not assessed; stopped at Part A. For the record, the identifiers present (Phytozome plant gene identifiers in Supplementary Table 4, rice variety names in Supplementary Table 3) would join to Phytozome and to RiceVarMap v2.0, but a join needs a table on our side and there is none.
integration.join_key: Phytozome gene identifiers (62 for OsALA5 orthologues, 58 for OsALIS2) and free-text rice variety names (36 rows). Variety names are free text, not standard accession codes, so they would need manual resolution.
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Not assessed: with 36 varieties on one side and no deposited phenotypes, no combined question can be written that the join would answer.

controls.positive_control: Not assessed; stopped at Part A. The paper does contain a natural one for any future model in this area: the catalytically dead OsALA5(D433N) mutant, which must show no lipid transport.
controls.external_validation: Not assessed. The paper's own cross-species checks (Arabidopsis ala9 to ala12 mutants, yeast dnf1 and dnf2 mutants) are the kind of independent replication a model would want, but they are a handful of panels, not a second dataset.

honest_claim_h3: Not assessed: stopped at Part A. No model can be trained from these files, so there is no claim to state.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a lipid pump's protein sequence to predict which fat molecule it moves and whether heat speeds it up.
plain_idea.train_on: This is the project I considered and could not build. Each example would be one lipid-flipping pump protein (a P4-ATPase) from a plant, fungus or animal, represented by its amino-acid sequence. Number of examples available from this paper: 62 rows naming rice OsALA5 lookalikes in other species, with no sequences and no measured cargo, so effectively zero usable examples.
plain_idea.predict: Which phospholipid class the pump prefers to move (phosphatidylcholine versus phosphatidylserine versus phosphatidylethanolamine) and whether that preference shifts when the temperature rises. The true answer would come from transport assays in which a fluorescently tagged lipid is fed to cells or to artificial vesicles and its uptake is timed; this paper reports such assays for exactly one pump at two temperatures.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Plant breeders and membrane biologists would use it to pick which of the dozens of uncharacterised pumps in a crop genome to test for heat protection, replacing a months-long assay per protein. Even a failed model would tell us whether cargo preference is readable from sequence at all, which is currently an open question.

ml_idea: There is no viable machine-learning project in this paper. It is a single-gene mechanistic study: it identifies one rice lipid pump, shows with about 35 small experiments that heat makes it move saturated phosphatidylcholine inward within minutes, and finds one favourable natural version of the gene. Its deposited data are the numbers behind each figure panel, laid out sideways, with 2 to 40 replicates per condition and no features. The two directions a modeller would want are both blocked: predicting pump cargo from sequence needs sequences and labels from the wider literature, not from here; and predicting rice heat tolerance from genotype needs the RiceVarMap v2.0 variety genotypes plus field phenotypes, neither of which this paper deposits (its haplotype survey only cites the database). If the topic is attractive, the route in is a literature-wide table of P4-ATPase transport assays joined to UniProt sequences, which would be a curation project first and a modelling project second.

effort.compute_note: Measured, not estimated: the six spreadsheets total 267,508 bytes and parsed in well under a second with the Python standard library. Hours-to-feature-table is null rather than a number because no feature table can be built at all, not because I failed to estimate one.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Already run, in about fifteen minutes: open the two Source Data workbooks and count. 15 sheets, 1,152 rows, 12,482 numeric cells spread over roughly 35 unrelated assays, laid out as figure panels with replicates running sideways across columns, and no column anywhere that is a prediction target. For any future mechanistic paper, this is the check: download the 'Source Data' file and look at whether it is a table or a stack of figure panels.

verdict_reason: Part A fails on A2, A3 and A5, all verified by opening the files. The deposited data are figure-panel source numbers (1,152 rows, 12,482 numeric cells across about 35 unrelated assays), not a dataset: there is no prediction-target column, no input features beyond a genotype nickname and a temperature, and no single task reaches even the 400-row classification floor. Units and label provenance are exemplary (every panel states its units; every number is a direct physical measurement), which is exactly why the failure is structural rather than fixable. No sequencing data was deposited anywhere, the paper's haplotype survey points at a third-party database, and the CC BY-NC-ND licence would complicate redistribution of any derived table.
